goal: Get comfortable with Rust ownership, borrowing and lifetimes so I can port a small Go CLI tool
interpretation: A senior Go dev can reason about moves, borrows and lifetimes, read borrow-checker errors, use traits, and write idiomatic Result/? error handling well enough to port a small Go CLI.
assumptions: Learner knows stack/heap and pointers, so the stack-vs-heap segment of the ownership video can be skimmed.
Generics and traits are only needed at the level required for trait bounds, dyn dispatch and error traits.
Async/Tokio is not needed for a small CLI.

sub_topics.why: Depth on the borrow checker was explicitly requested

picks.title: Understanding Ownership in Rust
picks.reason: Walks through moves, Copy, shared and mutable references and the borrow-checker rules with compiler error demos. Skim the early stack/heap section, which you already know.

evidence.quote: each value in rust has a variable that's called its owner so one variable one owner
instead of calculate length taking a string we'll make it take a reference to a string
you can only have one mutable reference to a particular piece of data in a particular scope

picks.confidence_note: Solid on the rules but somewhat beginner-paced at the start.

picks.title: Understanding Rust – Or How to Stop Worrying & Love the Borrow-Checker • Steve Smith • YOW! 2024
picks.reason: Conference talk that frames the compiler as a deterministic garbage collector, which suits a GC-language veteran. It covers lifetimes, Drop, Box, Rc and Send/Sync, which connect to your concurrency background.

evidence.quote: the compiler is your garbage collector. See all languages are garbage collected.
Rust can infer a lot of lifetimes, it can't infer all of them. Sometimes you need to make a promise to the Rust compiler.
RC allows you to create multiple pointers to something on the heap and each one of them is owned.

picks.confidence_note: Lecture format and light on code, but good depth on the model.

picks.title: Rust Lifetimes Finally Explained!
picks.reason: Covers lifetime annotations, the three elision rules, structs holding references and 'static, with worked examples.

evidence.quote: generic lifetime annotations describe the relationship between the lifetimes of multiple references and how they relate to each other
the lifetime of the returned reference will be the same as the smallest lifetime of the arguments
the compiler will try to follow these three rules and if at the end of these three rules it still can't figure out what the lifetimes are then we have to manually specify them
all string literals have a static lifetime and that's because string literals are stored in the program's binary

picks.confidence_note: Clear and complete on lifetime syntax.

picks.title: but what is 'a lifetime?
picks.reason: Gives a deeper mental model of what 'a means, using regions, liveness and subtyping. It fills the gap left by the official resources and builds the borrow-checker intuition you asked for.

evidence.quote: the problem is that the official rust learning resources only tell you about the particle interpretation leaving out half the picture
a reference really is just a special kind of pointer special because it has this tick a that the compiler uses to validate that the reference never points to invalid memory
what if instead of thinking about tick a as when the reference needs to be valid we thought of it as what the reference can point to

picks.confidence_note: Somewhat advanced and theory-heavy, but that is what the learner wants.

picks.title: Rust Powered Polymorphism ⚡️ With Traits
picks.reason: Compact comparison of traits with interfaces. It covers static dispatch with generics versus dyn dispatch, default methods and supertraits, which map onto Go interfaces.

evidence.quote: instead of interfaces Rust has something called traits which are very similar to interfaces but with some subtle differences
dyn refers to something called Dynamic dispatch which is in contrast to something called Static dispatch

picks.confidence_note: Short intro, but nothing better on traits was found for this level.

picks.title: Introduction to Generics and Traits | Advanced Rust Part 1
picks.reason: Adds trait bounds, Copy/Clone and implementing traits manually, tying them back to what the compiler enforces.

evidence.quote: traits or interfaces as they are called in most other languages are Concepts that guarantee that an object or struct provides a certain functionality
we need to make sure that the copy trait is implemented and we do this by adding the copy trait as a requirement for our type T

picks.confidence_note: Partly basic generics. Skim what Go generics already taught you.

picks.title: A Simpler Way to See Results
picks.reason: Presents Result as a sum type and covers the ? operator, collecting Results, error type design, From, and thiserror/anyhow. This is the mental model for replacing Go's err returns.

evidence.quote: result is a sum type just like all other enums in Rust
the question mark is a unary post-fix operator so you use it like this
if all the results are okay you get back an OK VEC but if any of them fails the whole thing fails
I would personally use the this error crate to derive a bunch of nice trait implementations all at once

picks.title: Mastering Error Handling in Rust: From Panics to thiserror & anyhow | with Nathan Stocks
picks.reason: Webinar that builds a CLI with Result, ? and a custom error enum, then adds thiserror and anyhow context. This is the practical idiomatic error handling a Go dev needs. I selected the core demo section.

evidence.quote: This does the exact same thing as that match expression. If the result is an okay, then it unwraps the inner value. If the result is an error variant, then it returns the error from the function.

result because result implements the termination trait. So, I've chosen to return one of any house results wrapping the unit type, which is just empty because we don't have anything useful to return in the success case.
we can use this errors error macro to derive the display and error traits. So let's check and see if we've got those.

picks.confidence_note: The timestamp window is estimated from quote times. The edges may start or end mid-topic.

picks.title: Build a Rust CLI Tool from Scratch (clap, serde, anyhow) – logscan
picks.reason: Short CLI build that hits a real E0515 borrow error with zero-copy parsing and fixes it by moving ownership up. It also shows anyhow and clap, which is close to your porting task.

evidence.quote: Time and message are string slices ampersand STR that borrow directly from the file's text instead of copying it. That's zero copy parsing and it's very fast.
The idiomatic fix, move ownership up. Let the caller own the text and only borrow from it. The string lives in main, which outlives everything else.
Data must live at least as long as anything that borrows it. When the borrow checker complains, ask yourself, who owns this, and does it live long enough?

picks.confidence_note: Fast-paced, but it applies the earlier material to a CLI.

Traits coverage is shallow, and no video on associated types, iterators or closures was found. The Rust Book chapter on traits would fill that gap.
Clap and argument parsing are only touched in the logscan video. There was no time to cover them fully.
